questions.q: What is a bin, in Tableau's terms?
options: A new dimension created by grouping a continuous measure's values into equal-sized ranges
A filter that removes all null values from a measure
A saved view that can be reused across worksheets
A type of calculated field that only works with dates
questions.explain: Creating a bin from a measure (via Create > Bins in the Data pane) converts its continuous values into a new dimension of equal-sized ranges.

questions.q: When is the histogram chart type available in Show Me?
options: Only when the view contains a single measure and no dimensions
Only after a bin has already been manually created
Only when connected to a live SQL Server connection
Histograms are never available through Show Me
questions.explain: Show Me surfaces the histogram option specifically when your current view has one measure and no dimensions — the minimum setup a histogram needs.

questions.q: What three things happen automatically when you build a histogram via Show Me?
options: The measure on Columns is replaced by a continuous bin dimension, the original measure moves to Rows, and its aggregation changes from SUM to CNT (Count)
The view is converted into a treemap, then reverted
All dimensions are removed and replaced with a single calculated field
The color palette switches to Red-Black Diverging automatically
questions.explain: Show Me swaps the raw measure for a bin dimension on Columns, moves the original measure to Rows, and switches its aggregation to Count — the defining structure of a histogram.

questions.q: What does the height of a bar in a histogram actually represent?
options: A count of how many rows fall within that bin's range of the original measure
The sum of the original measure's values within that bin
The average of the original measure across the entire dataset
The number of dimensions used to build the view
questions.explain: A histogram plots a count of rows per bin, not a sum — that's why the Rows shelf aggregation changes from SUM to CNT when building one.

questions.q: Why can two datasets share the exact same average value but still need to be told apart by their distributions?
options: Because a shared average can hide very different shapes — one dataset might cluster tightly around a typical value while another has multiple clusters or a long tail of outliers
Averages and distributions always describe identical information
Because Tableau calculates averages differently depending on bin size
Distributions only apply to date fields, not numeric measures
questions.explain: A single summary statistic like an average can't reveal whether data clusters near that value, splits into distinct groups, or is skewed by outliers — a histogram's shape is what shows that.
